I am writing to suggest the addition of a new category for CI/CD security risks in the ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard). Currently, the ASVS does not explicitly cover security risks related to CI/CD pipelines, which are becoming increasingly important in modern software development.

As more organizations adopt continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) practices, it is essential that the ASVS includes guidance on how to verify the security of these pipelines. CI/CD pipelines are often used to automate the deployment of software, which means that vulnerabilities in these pipelines can lead to the rapid deployment of insecure code.

A dedicated category for CI/CD security risks in the ASVS would provide developers and security professionals with clear guidance on how to identify and mitigate these risks. This would help to improve the overall security of software systems and reduce the likelihood of successful attacks.

Therefore, I would like to request that the ASVS Development Team consider adding a new category for CI/CD security risks in a future release of the standard. This would be a valuable addition to the ASVS and would help to ensure that it remains relevant and useful for modern software development practices.
We can get inspired by OWASP Top 10 CI/CD Security Risks framework to create related ASVS issues.
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/78227895/222478683-eba8bd41-94f5-49a0-8131-d112c0c972f9.png)

These are my recommendations for the Insufficient Flow Control Mechanisms subcategory. If the ASVS team chooses not to include a CI/CD security category, I will establish a new OWASP project dedicated to CI/CD Security Verification Standards. @jmanico @elarlang

- Verify that branch protection rules are configured on branches hosting code used in production and other sensitive systems, with no exclusions for user accounts or branches without a valid reason.
- Verify that auto-merge rules are limited in usage, thoroughly reviewed, and not bypassable. Ensure auto-merge rules do not import third-party code without proper scrutiny.Verify that user accounts with permission to push unreviewed code to a repository are restricted from triggering deployment pipelines connected to the repository.
- Verify that production build and deployment pipelines require additional approval or review before being triggered by any account.
- Verify that artifacts are only allowed to flow through the pipeline if created by a pre-approved CI service account. Ensure secondary review and approval is required for artifacts uploaded by other accounts.Verify that drifts and inconsistencies between code running in production and its CI/CD origin are detected and prevented. Implement mechanisms to modify any resource containing a drift.
- Verify that the CI/CD pipeline implements a multi-step approval process for deploying code and artifacts to sensitive environments, including production.Verify that pipeline flow control mechanisms are in place to detect and prevent unauthorized changes to application code or infrastructure in production environments.
- Verify that access to the SCM, CI, and artifact repository systems is restricted to authorized users and applications with the principle of least privilege applied.Verify that all changes to production code and infrastructure undergo a strict set of reviews and approvals, including peer review, security review, and change management approval.
- Verify that the CI/CD pipeline has an audit log to track and monitor all actions performed, including code pushes, pipeline triggers, and artifact deployments.
- Verify that continuous monitoring and alerting mechanisms are in place to detect suspicious activity in the CI/CD pipeline and trigger appropriate incident response procedures.
